content.text: The channels shift with the season, and a route safe in March is not always a route safe in September. The last light in the house went out later that winter than in any winter before it. An unopened letter waits with a patience its writer rarely shared.

I have never fully trusted solid ground since spending a summer learning how little of the fen actually qualifies. The bakery's ovens stayed warm long after closing, heating the whole street a little further into the evening. A long-kept promise is worth more, if anything, for having been long-kept.

The last ferry crossing became, over the years, less a boat ride and more a small, reliable ritual. The harbor emptied of boats by storm warning and filled again, cautiously, the following noon. An old friend recognized across a crowded market is a small, entirely disproportionate joy.

Wanderings beyond the fen always end the same way, with the willow line closing quietly behind you like a door. The workshop's ledgers, taken together, told a quieter story than either the profits or the losses alone. A garden wall built by hand outlasts, as a rule, the hands that built it.

Beyond the willow line the fen forgets, almost entirely, that a town exists a half day's walk away. Time moves at a different pace when there is work enough to fill it entirely. A room remembers its last occupant longer than most people expect.

The last ferry crossing of the day left at dusk, and I have never since managed to be anywhere but late for it. The kettle took its usual three minutes, and in that time the whole morning seemed to settle. Distance is measured in more than miles once you have walked enough of it yourself.

A heron's shadow on the water is often the only warning the fen offers before the light actually changes. A garden left untended for a season still remembers, mostly, what it was planted to become. The clock in the hall ran two minutes fast for as long as anyone could remember, and no one corrected it.

We poled the flat-bottomed boat through channels that closed behind us as reliably as they opened ahead. Patience is easier to recommend than to practise, a fact every teacher of it eventually admits. The correspondence between old friends thins with distance but rarely stops outright.

The willow line marks where the solid ground gives up any pretence of being solid. A machine well maintained will forgive a great many small mistakes; one neglected forgives none. Quiet, in the right house, is not an absence of sound but a particular kind of company.

A ferryman who has crossed the same channel for thirty years reads it the way other men read a familiar room. The weather that season did exactly what the almanac predicted, which surprised everyone involved. A long walk clarifies more than a long conversation, in my limited experience of both.

Beyond the willows the birds outnumber the people by a margin no one has ever bothered to count precisely. The light in late afternoon has a habit of making ordinary rooms look briefly important. Memory keeps the details it wants and discards the ones it decides, later, were never essential.

The last crossing ran even in fog, on the theory that the ferryman knew the channel better than the fog did. A well-kept ledger tells you less about money than it does about the person who kept it. The city at that hour belonged mostly to delivery carts and the occasional insomniac.

I have walked the fen in every season and trust it least, oddly, in the gentlest weather. Old letters, reread, always sound slightly more confident than the person who wrote them actually was. A door left ajar in an old house creaks in a key entirely its own.

A causeway built a century ago still holds, mostly, though the fen has reclaimed both its ends. The harvest that year came in later than usual, and no less welcome for it. Silence between two people who know each other well is rarely uncomfortable.

The willow line hums with insects by July in a way that makes conversation, past a certain hour, pointless. The workshop light stayed on past midnight more nights than either of us cared to count. A path worn into a lawn tells you exactly where people actually wanted the path to be.

We watched the last ferry pull away without us once, and walked the long way round rather than shout after it. The sea keeps no calendar, which is either its great honesty or its great indifference. An old friend visiting after years away brings the past with them, uninvited but not unwelcome.

A fen at dawn is quieter than a fen at dusk, though I have never been able to explain the difference convincingly. The bread was better that winter, though no one could say exactly why. A long apprenticeship teaches humility faster than it teaches skill, and in the correct order.

The ferryman's fee, like the salt trader's, was sometimes a story rather than a coin, if the story was good enough. The train timetable was more aspiration than fact, and everyone along the line understood as much. A candle burns down evenly only if you trim the wick, a lesson repeated in every household.

Beyond the willow line the map, such as it is, gives up and simply writes fen across the rest of the page. The orchard gave less fruit that year but of a better, denser sweetness. A stranger's kindness on a hard day is remembered longer than most kindnesses from family.

A single lantern on the far bank told us the last crossing still ran, some nights, later than advertised. The wind off the water carried salt far enough inland to whiten the window glass by spring. A journal kept honestly becomes, without meaning to, a kind of second memory.

The market emptied by four, leaving only the smell of what had been sold there. An old dog knows the sound of the right footsteps long before anyone else in the house does. The harvest moon that year hung low enough to seem, briefly, close.

A debt repaid on time is remembered less than one repaid a day late. The workshop smelled of sawdust and, faintly, of the coffee no one ever finished. A letter that arrives too late still says something true, even if the moment has passed.

The garden wall held the day's heat long after the sun itself had gone down. An empty house is loud in a way a full one never manages to be. The apprentice years pass slowly at the time and quickly in the remembering.

A well-worn tool fits the hand better than any new one, however well made. The evening train was always half empty, and always exactly on time. An old photograph tells you what a person looked like and almost nothing about who they were.

The bakery opened before the rest of the street had decided the day had begun. A long correspondence, kept up faithfully, is its own kind of small monument. The frost came early that year and stripped the orchard almost overnight.

An honest account of a hard season reads, afterward, like a much easier one than it was. The workshop door stuck in wet weather, a fault no one ever quite got around to fixing. A river town keeps different hours than a market town, and neither much minds the other's.
